did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with Moses conveying to the Israelites the words as the Lord commanded, emphasizing the obligation to remain faithful to the divine command.
Moses addresses the heads of the tribes in particular and presents the command to them. This highlights the role of the tribal leaders in transmitting the instruction to the people.
The Torah states that anyone who makes a vow or takes an oath to prohibit something to themselves must fulfill their word: “Whatever they have spoken, they must do.”

The vows of a young woman living in her father’s household depend on her father’s response: if he hears them and does not object on the day he hears them, the vows and obligations she has taken upon herself remain valid.
The young woman’s father may annul her vow on the day he hears about it. In that case, the vow does not stand, and the verse states that the Lord will forgive her.
When a woman makes a vow before she is married, her vows remain valid unless her husband annuls them on the day he hears about them.
The vows of a widow or a divorced woman remain valid, since the verse does not assign a father or husband the authority to annul them.
According to the chapter, in vows and oaths intended to afflict a person, the husband may uphold the vow or annul it.
The husband’s silence after hearing his wife’s vows upholds them; if he annuls them after the time specified in the verse, he bears her guilt.
At the end of the chapter, the Torah summarizes that these laws concern the relationship between a man and his wife and between a father and his young daughter living in her father’s household.
